projects.name: Morph
projects.tagline: Every robot sim lets you command a robot. None let you change one, so "it can't reach" means editing URDF by hand. Morph: say "make the arm 20cm longer" and it rebuilds, live.
projects.note: 'Make the forearm 20cm longer' rebuilds the URDF and hot-reloads keeping joint state, then you re-run the command that just failed. Fixes a real robotics pain nobody else touched.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every robot simulator lets you command a robot. None of them let you change one.
So the moment the arm can't reach the top shelf, you leave the tool. You open the URDF in a text editor, edit the XML by hand, recompute inertias, push all the child joints out, and hope the origins still line up. Reload, find out you got the rpy wrong, do it again.
Redesign is the loop. Reach, fail, make the arm longer, try again. We wanted that to be a sentence instead of an afternoon.
The setup cost around it doesn't help either. Doing one thing in simulation usually means installing ROS, fighting Gazebo, writing a URDF by hand, and scripting a controller before anything moves at all. It's tooling built for people who already know robotics, which is a problem if you're trying to learn it.
What it does
Drop in a URDF and it renders as a live 3D model with the full joint tree, limits, and an end effector you can drag around with IK. Upload your own or pick one from the library.
Then you talk to it. There are two kinds of things you can say.
The first kind changes what the robot does. "Pick up the green cube and stack it on the blue block." "Drive forward for 3 seconds, turn 90 degrees left, repeat 4 times." "Move forward at 0.5 m/s until the front sensor sees something within 30 cm, then avoid it." The planner gets a live JSON view of the scene with joint angles, object poses, and distances, and sends back a validated action graph instead of prose. The sim runs it.
The second kind changes what the robot is. "Add a parallel gripper to the wrist." "Extend the forearm by 20 cm." "Let the elbow rotate further." The model gets rebuilt and hot reloads in place, keeping whatever joint state it was already in. Then you run the command that just failed and watch it work.
Scenes work the same way. Describe one in a sentence, like a 3x3 warehouse grid with four red hazard cubes and a blue loading dock in the far corner, or place things by hand with drag and drop.

projects.name: Sharingan
projects.tagline: Every door is a guess. Not anymore. This is a real wallhack,  a $600 drone system that finds people through walls and floors, streamed live to a VR headset.
projects.note: Drone that finds people through walls, streamed to a Quest 3S. They pull the network cable mid-flight on camera to prove the link is air-gapped. Best pure demo theater in the gallery.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every year floods, earthquakes, and building collapses put rescuers in the same position: they know people are trapped somewhere inside, but not where, and every door they open blind costs time they don't have. We wanted a scout drone that could fly in ahead of a rescue team and tell them who's inside and where before anyone crosses the threshold.
The same problem shows up outside disaster response. A soldier clearing a room, a SWAT team going through a doorway, a firefighter deciding which door to breach first, all of them are making the same blind call under time pressure about what's on the other side. We built for search and rescue first because the stakes are the cleanest there, you're trying to save someone. But the core problem, knowing what's on the other side before a person has to find out the hard way, is the same one soldiers and first responders deal with every time they clear a structure.
What it does
SHARINGAN is a scout drone that flies ahead of a person, finds people through walls, floors, and openings using onboard computer vision and radar, and streams what it sees to a Meta Quest 3S headset worn by the operator, live, as an annotated tactical view. There's no cloud and no dependency on venue Wi-Fi. The link is wired and air-gapped, and we prove it on camera by pulling the network cable mid-flight and showing the feed keeps running.
The drone detects people, tracks them on its own, and relays their position to the ground in real time. That's the part that makes it actually usable in the moment instead of just interesting sensor data: the operator isn't staring at a laptop trying to interpret a feed, they're looking through the headset at tracked positions overlaid on the space in front of them. Know who's where before you decide what to do next. If a detection goes stale, the HUD says so, "SENSOR OFFLINE," instead of freezing on a last known frame and quietly lying to the operator. projects.name: PiHive
projects.tagline: Datacenter on a desk: cloud LLMs see your data and charge per token; local LLMs need pricey hardware. We split a model across $100 Raspberry Pis for machines too weak to run it alone run it together.
projects.note: Raspberry Pi cluster running one LLM tensor-parallel behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, escalating to an H100 on Baseten — then uses that H100 to distill the small model. X-Served-By header as proof.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Every AI coding agent we use fires off hundreds of LLM requests a day, and every single one leaves the machine. Your prompts, your files, your half-finished code — all of it goes to the cloud, and you pay per token for the privilege, even when the request is "write a for loop."
The alternative is local inference, but that's gated on hardware: a useful model won't fit on any single cheap device, so "local AI" in practice means "buy a GPU."
We noticed the big labs solved this with a pattern — Apple Intelligence and Gemini Nano both run a small model on-device and silently escalate hard requests to a big model in the cloud. But their version requires custom silicon: Neural Engines, TPUs. We wondered: could you get the same architecture out of the cheapest computers you can buy, ganged together?
So we put a datacenter on a desk.
What it does
PiHive
is a cluster of Raspberry Pis running one LLM together via tensor-parallel distributed inference, no GPU anywhere, behind a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint. A router decides where each request belongs:
Simple requests stay local
— served by the cluster, private and free
Heavy requests escalate to an H100 on Baseten
— long context, hard reasoning
Frontier-class agentic work escalates to the OpenAI API
Point Claude Code or Warp at the endpoint and it just works. The client never knows which tier answered — except for the 
X-Served-By
header that proves it.
The twist: the H100 isn't just the fallback. It's the 
teacher
. We used it to distill the large model into the small one running on the Pis — generated thousands of coding-agent-style training examples from the big model, then LoRA fine-tuned the small one on its outputs. The same GPU that handles the requests our cluster can't is the reason our cluster can handle any at all.

projects.name: Agentigram
projects.tagline:
Git tracks history... Agentigram prevents collisions. 

We virtual-merge uncommitted agent code, force AIs to negotiate contracts, and let devs bet play-money on which model survives the build.
projects.note: Virtual-merges uncommitted code across agents on different laptops and forces them to negotiate interface contracts over MCP. Derives a collision-probability model to justify itself.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Autonomous coding agents (such as Claude Code, Cursor, and Aider) have dramatically increased individual developer velocity. However, software engineering remains fundamentally cooperative. Git was architected in 2005 for asynchronous, human-paced collaboration—engineers branch, write code, commit, and reconcile conflicts hours or days later through pull requests.
When multiple autonomous agents operate concurrently on local machines, this paradigm breaks down mathematically. If \(n\) distributed agents mutate a shared codebase with an average modification rate of \(\lambda\) edits per minute, the probability of concurrent, overlapping mutations on common symbol dependency sets scales as:
$$P(\text{collision}) = 1 - \exp\left(-\binom{n}{2} \lambda \tau\right)$$
where \(\tau\) is the latency between an agent's initial file read and its ultimate pull request integration. In traditional workflows, \(\tau \gg 0\), causing semantic merge conflicts to compound undetected in volatile working memory.
We built 
Clankergram
to replace blind, post-hoc conflict resolution with real-time speculative coordination. Clankergram observes agent read/write telemetry across distributed laptops, computes virtual merges and type checks on uncommitted code, forces colliding agents to negotiate interface contracts over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and makes observability engaging through a play-money prediction league.
What it does
Clankergram acts as an active coordination layer positioned between distributed agent runtimes and the source repository:
Passive Telemetry Daemon:
A lightweight local daemon monitors file buffers, active AST symbol ranges, and prompt intentions across each developer's laptop without interrupting normal workflows.
Speculative Merge & AST Typechecking:
Before any local code is committed or pushed, the coordinator executes in-memory virtual merges across dirty working trees, running incremental typechecks to surface semantic breakages immediately.

projects.name: Blimpy
projects.tagline: A helium companion that follows you, talks, and keeps you focused.
projects.note: A helium companion that follows you and keeps you focused. Floats over a judging floor, which is worth more than it sounds.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Indoor drones are loud, heavy, and a little scary. We wanted a robot that could share a room with people: near-silent, soft when it bumps you, and useful as a companion rather than a gadget. A helium balloon is almost that already. It floats, it is quiet, and if you trim it a gram heavy it sinks gently to the floor when the power dies. The catch is that its lift drifts by the gram as the room warms and helium leaks, so the brain has to keep adapting to the air. That made it interesting.
What it does
Blimpy is a helium-balloon robot that follows you around a room, talks, and helps you focus.
You speak, it answers. "Follow me" and it holds about 1.5 m away, facing you. "Stop" and it hovers in place, even under the air conditioning. "Come here", "go show the judges", "wander", "turn left", "you're too high", and more, all map to their own behaviours. It sets timers, runs a pomodoro, dances on request, and runs a focus guard: while you work it glances at the desk every few seconds and nags you when you drift onto your phone. Ask "what do you see?" and it tells you, because the same model that hears you also looks through its eye.
How we built it
One rule: the laptop thinks, the gondola is a motor box.
The Body: Four tiny reversible motors on a 1.1 m latex balloon: two at the back for drive and turning, one sideways to kill drift, one vertical to hold height. It is trimmed one gram heavy so a dead Blimpy lands instead of hiding on the ceiling. The laptop sends body-frame velocity commands twenty times a second; a Bluetooth bridge turns them into motor percentages and streams the gyro and altitude back. Any silence longer than half a second stops every motor.
The physics: A balloon is not a drone. It weighs almost nothing on a scale but drags half its displaced air along, so it resists acceleration and coasts for metres after the motors stop. projects.name: Parity / BadgeCraft
projects.tagline: Parity migrates your code to a new language with a team of AI agents that proves nothing broke. BadgeCraft is Minecraft on our hacker badges :)
projects.note: Proves a Python→Rust migration is semantically identical on a hidden input set. Their hook — -1//1000 is -1 in Python, 0 in Rust — is a better demo than most whole projects. Two entries in one.
projects.body:
The problem
A lot of the world runs on old code that nobody wants to touch. Companies want it in Rust for speed and memory safety, and they don't do it because a rewrite is months of work and one wrong edge case takes down production.
AI can now do the rewriting in minutes but that didn't solve the problem. The hard part was never typing the new code. It's knowing the new code does the same thing as the old code.
Here is the kind of bug we mean. In Python, 
-1 // 1000
is 
-1
. In Rust, 
-1 / 1000
is 
0
. A model translates one into the other, the code compiles, the obvious tests pass, and every timestamp before 1970 now lands in the wrong bucket. Nobody notices for a year.
What it does
You point Parity at a Python file, a folder, or the name of a PyPI package. It scans the code and lists every function as "can migrate" or "can't", with the reason (touches files, reads the clock, shared state, and so on).
Then the agent team rewrites them in Rust, one function at a time. A function is only kept when a checker has run the old code and the new code on the same inputs and every answer matches. At the end, a hidden set of inputs that no agent ever saw is run once. You get a patch, a report, and for every function either "proven" or "needs a human, and here is the input it fails on".

projects.name: Quorum
projects.tagline: every approval was correct. The purchase still shouldn't have happened.
projects.note: Two agents disagree on purpose; blocks a $9,400 request in 15ms and names the four prior POs that make it $47,200 across cost centers. Zero dependencies, no API keys, deterministic routing.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Approval limits assume a human pace and a human field of view. An approver sees their own queue and nothing else — so five requests, each honestly under a $10,000 limit, each approved by a different manager in a different cost center, can add up to a $47,200 purchase that policy says needs VP sign-off. No fraud, no bad actor, nobody doing anything wrong. The blindness is structural. I wanted to build the approver that reads across queues.
What it does
Quorum ingests messy purchase requests and adjudicates them against both the rulebook and everything else in flight.
Two agents disagree on purpose. The 
Policy agent
judges the request in isolation, like a human approver would — and it's 
correct
when it says APPROVE. The 
Pattern agent
pulls the context nobody has and runs four detectors: split purchases across cost centers, vendor contract-ceiling drift, double-committed budgets, and usage-based run-rate. An 
Adjudicator
resolves the conflict and emits an audit record — decision, confidence, rule IDs, and the specific PO IDs that prove it — then writes it back.
The flagship case blocks a $9,400 request in 15ms and names the four prior orders that bring the total to $47,200.
How we built it
Python, zero dependencies, runs with no API keys. Topology is 
normalize → (policy ‖ pattern) → adjudicate → write back
, orchestrated by plain code — the routing is fixed and knowable, so an LLM router would cost determinism for nothing.
Two rules: 
the model never decides
(the verdict is a deterministic function of the policy check and the findings; the model only writes the explanation), and 
every agent has a deterministic floor
(the LLM pass is an enhancement that can be disagreed with, never a dependency). The four detectors are pure functions with 20 unit tests.

Entity resolution turned out to be the whole product.

projects.name: Cadabra
projects.tagline: Frontier models can produce CAD designs from engineering only 61% of the time. We post-trained a 4B model to do it BETTER, FASTER and CHEAPER it would make you say abraCADabra!!
projects.body:
Inspiration
Frontier models are becoming extremely good at writing code, but we wanted to find a narrow engineering task where a smaller specialized model could still compete.
We initially explored text-to-CAD, where a model receives a written description of a part and generates the CadQuery code needed to build it. Before training anything, we tested frontier models on the task. Kimi K3 correctly generated 95% of our held-out parts from text, which showed us that the problem was already close to solved.
Real CAD work, however, rarely begins with a perfectly written specification. Engineers usually work from drawings. When we replaced the text descriptions with drawing sheets containing front, top, right, and isometric views, Kimi K3 dropped to 61% accuracy. On complex parts, both Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 Flash fell as low as 22.5%.
That gap inspired Understudy-CAD: a small vision model specialized in converting engineering drawings directly into executable CAD programs.
What it does
Understudy-CAD takes an engineering drawing sheet and the part's bounding-box dimensions as input. It generates CadQuery code, executes that code, and produces a real 3D solid.
The system can sample multiple candidate programs and check its own work without accessing the correct answer. Each candidate is rendered from the same views as the original drawing, then compared against the input sheet. Understudy keeps the candidate whose shape and dimensions best match the drawing.
We also built a live 3D race that compares Understudy against Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3 Flash on held-out parts. Each lane displays the generated object overlaid on the target, along with its accuracy, latency, token usage, and cost.
How we built it
We started with CAD-Coder, an open dataset containing CadQuery programs and their corresponding text specifications. We executed the reference programs and rendered each part into a standardized drawing sheet containing three orthographic views and one isometric view.

projects.name: Consentinel
projects.tagline: Your badge blinks a coded light that says if you consent to being filmed. Cameras running Consentinel see it and blur the faces of anyone who opted out.
projects.note: Your badge blinks a coded light and cameras blur you if you opted out. A real consent primitive, on-theme for the badge.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Hack the North puts a couple thousand people in a few rooms with a camera pointed at almost all of them, almost all the time: livestreams, photographers, other people's vlogs, phones. Nobody asks, and there's no way to say no. Recording consent today is a checkbox you never saw, buried in a policy you didn't read.
The spark of inspiration was the badge itself. This year's HTN badge is an ESP32 with a screen, buttons, and a radio - a tiny computer you're already wearing. We realized it could 
announce who you are as a beam of light
, and that a camera could read that beam and respect your choice frame by frame. Your consent stops being a form you sign once and becomes something you carry, show, and revoke, enforced by light and owned by you.
What it does
Consentinel is a consent layer for a camera. People wear the HTN badge, which blinks a coded light pattern carrying a short ID. A capture app films the scene and, in near-real-time:
Decodes the light beacons
out of the video to recover each badge's ID.
Detects faces
and links each badge to the nearest face above it (badges are chest-worn).
Blurs the faces of people who haven't consented
to being filmed and blurs anyone it's unsure about.
Consent is a 
signed, revocable record you own on Solana
, keyed to your badge. The camera reads your consent from that record, never from your face. When someone who opted out is captured, their badge lights a red alert and a spoken notice plays, so a violation is felt, not buried in a log.
Two properties are important to mention:
No face database.
We never identify anyone by their face. Identity comes from the light beacon; the face is used only to know 
where
to blur, and that box is discarded every frame. A privacy tool must not itself build a faceprint store.
Fail-safe by default.
If a face has no readable badge, or consent is unknown, it gets blurred. The safe state is the resting state; you become visible only by actively presenting a consenting badge.

projects.name: Dealify
projects.tagline: An AI shopkeeper for Shopify: shoppers make an offer, code protects the merchant's margin, and accepted deals lead to Shopify Checkout. Test pricing policies with 300 synthetic shoppers.
projects.note: An AI shopkeeper that haggles while code protects the merchant's margin, tested against 300 synthetic shoppers. Written directly at Shopify's brief.
projects.body:
Inspiration
When a shopper likes a product but cannot justify the price, they usually leave. A store's usual answer is a sale for everyone, including customers who would have paid full price.
We wanted to bring the conversation of a market stall to online shopping: make an offer, explain what you need, and find a deal that works for both sides. The hard part was giving an AI that role without giving it control over a merchant's money.
What it does
Dealify is an AI shopkeeper for Shopify, built in our Bazaar repository and demonstrated in the Trailhead store. Shoppers ask product questions, name a price, and negotiate through offer cards directly on a product page.
The server considers the product's cost, stock age, negotiation round, and buyer context. It can hold the price, counter, or suggest a bundle. Repeating a low offer does not automatically unlock the lowest price. The card shows the actual offer and its expiry; accepting it starts the Shopify discount-code and checkout flow.
We also built the Gym simulation engine. It runs 300 seeded, rule-based synthetic shoppers against a pricing policy and compares the result with a 20%-off banner. It reports outcomes such as purchases, profit, bundles, and missed deals. These are reproducible simulations, not revenue predictions or real customer results.
How we built it
The live storefront is a Shopify Liquid theme with a JavaScript chat widget. A Node.js server on Railway reads Shopify product, variant, inventory, and cost data through the Admin GraphQL API. Gemini handles product Q&A, while deterministic server code controls the offer amounts. Accepted offers use single-use Shopify discount codes and cart permalinks.
Alongside that live path, we built reusable TypeScript packages for shared contracts, pricing, and the Gym. projects.name: MExT
projects.tagline: Stop asking one world model to do everything. Start routing to the one that's actually good at it.
projects.note: A router for robot policies instead of one generalist — OpenRouter's idea applied to control. Two 4-DOF arms physically hand off to demonstrate it.
projects.body:
Tl;dr, MExT is jarvis for everyone.
Inspiration
Every "generalist" AI robot policy we looked at made the same trade-off: one model trying to
be good at everything, navigation, grasping, fine manipulation, ends up being merely
okay at all of it, or incredibly compute heavy. We kept coming back to a pattern the LLM world already solved: OpenRouter doesn't force one model to handle every kind of text query, it routes each request to whichever model is actually best suited for it. Thus, our project comes in, [name].
What it does
Our system is a router for robotic control: instead of one generalized policy driving every
joint on every task, a router observes the task at hand and dispatches it to the specialized
policy best suited to execute it, the same way you'd call a surgeon for stitches and a
weightlifter to move something heavy.
We built two 4-DOF robotic arms that physically demonstrate this: rather than one model
controlling both arms identically, our router assigns each arm the specialized behavior its
moment in the task calls for, so they can cooperate, handing off, coordinating timing, and
adapting their individual movement style to what the shared task actually needs, in ways a
single generalized model visibly struggles to do as cleanly.
This comes with several benefits, which include (but are not limited to):
Hardware costs and ease of setup
. The hardware benefits of doing it in this manner, for the consumer, are vast. We're able to be able to run an entire world model off of any tiny microcontroller with internet access, requiring almost nothing in terms of actual specs, vastly cutting down on both setup times and compute/hardware costs by offloading it to the cloud.
1b. 
Modularity

projects.name: Kosmos
projects.tagline: A ruler for robot policies. We rank them inside a world model on Baseten instead of on hardware, check the ranking against 1,500 human-scored real trials, and then measure its precision.
projects.note: Ranks robot policies inside a world model, then treats its own leaderboard as an instrument and measures whether the ranking repeats. The only team in the gallery that checked its own precision.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Comparing two robot control models — the AI that decides how a robot arm moves — costs a person a week. The benchmark of record in this field took fifteen hundred real robot trials to produce six numbers: a dedicated arm, a human scoring every single attempt, and twenty-minute cooldowns because the motors overheat. That is why the field compares six models and not six hundred.
The usual escape hatch is a physics simulator, and the same study shows it failing badly. On one model closing a drawer, humans scored ninety-two percent and the simulator scored four. Trust the simulator and you throw away a model that works nine times in ten.
Three groups have already automated this using generative world models. We read all three. Every one of them checked whether their ranking matches reality. Not one checked whether the ranking comes out the same twice.
That is the gap. Picture a bathroom scale that reads seventy, then seventy-four, then sixty-six. It averages out correct and it is still useless.
What it does
Kosmos ranks robot control models without using a robot.
You type a task in plain language. The model under test looks at the scene and decides how to move. Instead of sending that command to real hardware, we send it to a video world model, which generates what the next moment would look like. Repeat the loop and you have a recording of an attempt that never happened. A judge then scores it — first a deterministic check that throws out physically impossible video, then a graded rubric over what survives.
The output is a leaderboard. The leaderboard is not the point. We treated our own leaderboard as an instrument under test and measured four things we could not find published anywhere:
Does it repeat? Split the attempts in half and see whether both halves produce the same ranking.
How small a difference can it see? Below some gap, two models are indistinguishable inside our own noise. We report where that line sits instead of pretending it does not exist

projects.name: Cardboard Cockpit
projects.tagline: Eliminating hardware tax on flight sims. Saving you $500+
projects.body:
Inspiration
Everyone who has ever wanted to fly a fighter jet runs into the same wall: the hardware tax. A decent HOTAS setup costs $300–$500. A VR headset costs more. Flight sim is one of the oldest genres in gaming and it is still gated behind a pile of plastic that most people will never buy.
Meanwhile, the highest-bandwidth input device most of us already own is a webcam — and it sits there doing nothing but video calls.
So we asked a stupid question: what is the cheapest possible cockpit? The answer we landed on was a sheet of paper. Print some markers, fold a yoke, hold it up, and let the camera do the work. Cardboard is the only material on Earth that costs nothing, is infinitely reconfigurable, and that everyone already has in a recycling bin.
And once we had a jet, it needed something to shoot at. We went with a giant goose.
What it does
Goose Protocol — SPECTRE X-26 is a native desktop flight simulator you control with printed cardboard and a webcam. No drivers, no VR, no controller.
The cardboard yoke owns pitch, roll and both latched weapon switches
The cardboard throttle owns power, boost and braking
A wireless BLE badge handles secondary controls — start, pause, gear, assisted landing, camera views
Keyboard and mouse always work, and always take priority the instant you touch them
You fly a real, photogrammetrically sourced San Francisco — SFO, downtown, the residential grid, the hills, the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges, Alcatraz — on a mission that escalates from routine intercepts to an anomalous signature, and then to a 16,000-HP boss goose with staged weak regions.
The entire demo — takeoff, city run, escalation, boss, aftermath, assisted landing at SFO — is capped at 150 seconds. Unlimited ammunition, forgiving flight assistance, spoken in-mission coaching that hands control back to you after the first three contacts, and crash recovery that puts you back into stable flight instead of a loading screen. projects.name: Auto-selfie
projects.tagline: You tell it how you want your photo to look, it moves to the perfect spot to take it.
projects.note: A camera that walks itself to the right spot. Fun, narrow, and hard to read as more than a gag.
projects.body:
Inspiration
The idea came from a family trip. We watched our parents struggle to take a single decent photo — one of them squinting at the screen, backing up into strangers, trying to get both the whole family 
and
the landmark behind us into frame. Meanwhile my brother and I stood frozen in a pose for two minutes, blocking a footpath while everyone else waited for us to finish.
Tripods don't fix this. A tripod holds a camera still, but composing a shot against a specific background needs someone 
behind
the camera who can move it — and someone telling you where to put your arm. We wanted to build the person behind the camera.
What it does
Auto-selfie is a small autonomous rover that photographs you.
You place it down, wake it with a raised hand, and say what you want out loud:
"Frame me next to the big tree"
→ a standard rule-of-thirds composition, you on one third, the tree on the other
"Make me point at the bird"
→ the same framing, plus it coaches your arm until you're actually pointing at the bird
It then drives itself into position, tilts the phone, tells you to shift your hand up or left if it needs to, counts you down, and takes the shot. You never touch anything.
The key insight that makes it work: 
driving the camera and zooming do different things.
Moving the rover changes perspective — how big the background looks next to you — while zoom only changes overall size. That splits an intimidating "compose a photo" problem into four independent, controllable axes: turn, drive, tilt, crop.
The second insight: 
the rover never tracks where it is.
It has no wheel encoders and no map. You are its coordinate system. Your shoulder width in pixels is its distance measurement, re-measured fresh in every single frame, so nothing drifts, ever.
How we built it
Three pieces talking over one Wi-Fi network:
Phone (the eye)
— an iPhone mounted 
backwards
on the rover, facing you. It runs a single HTML page in Safari, served over HTTPS by the laptop. No app install. The page

projects.name: Aria - A non-linear voice browser.
projects.tagline: Empowering visually impaired users to skip endless tabbing. Hold a key and use natural language to instantly navigate and interact with the web.
projects.note: Hold a key and speak to jump anywhere on a page instead of tabbing through it. Real accessibility gain with a tight demo.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Have you ever watched someone navigate the web using a standard screen reader? It's incredibly frustrating to witness. They are forced to experience a 2D webpage as a 1D, linear string of text. To find a single "Checkout" button, they might have to mash the 'Tab' key 50 times to get past the nav bar and sidebars.
We realized that forcing a visually impaired user to "find" a button when they already know exactly what they want to do is a complete failure of UX. We wanted to build something that lets them skip the tabbing and just talk directly to the DOM.

You hold the Spacebar, say "Click the download PDF button," and release. Aria instantly finds the exact element on the page and clicks it for you.

Smart Disambiguation:
If you say "Download" and there are two identical download buttons, the system doesn't just guess and risk breaking your workflow. It pauses, highlights both, and asks you a clarifying question to make sure it gets it right.

projects.body:
Inspiration
Navigation apps are built for sighted users: maps, arrows, and screens assume you can see the world around you. For blind and low-vision pedestrians, a turn-by-turn instruction is only half the problem—the other half is what is directly in front of me right now?
EchoPath started from a simple question: what if the phone you already carry could do both? Modern iPhones ship with LiDAR, precise motion sensors, spatial audio, and haptics. That hardware is powerful, but it is rarely wired together into a single, accessibility-first walking experience.
We were inspired by orientation-and-mobility (O&M) practice—where a cane or guide dog gives immediate tactile feedback about the path ahead—and by the idea that technology should supplement, not replace, those tools. EchoPath is not a safety certification system. It is a prototype that explores how real-time sensing, calm audio cues, and clear information hierarchy can help someone walk with more confidence.
What We Learned
Safety-critical systems must be local-first
Cloud AI is excellent for rewriting phrases or synthesizing natural speech, but it cannot sit in the immediate warning path. Network latency, API failures, and rate limits are unacceptable when someone is mid-step.
We learned to split the stack:
Local (milliseconds): LiDAR analysis, lane decisions, spatial tones, haptics
Cloud (supplemental): OpenAI phrase rewriting, ElevenLabs TTS, optional image context
Obstacle warnings always preempt route guidance. If sensors fail, the app says so—silence is worse than an honest error.
Audio design is a UX problem, not just an engineering one

Right

Short pulse, right-weighted

projects.body:
Inspiration
I kept seeing reactions to a post without knowing what people were reacting to. Breaking-news claims, explanations, criticism, and jokes can all be part of one conversation, yet a search feed scatters them across days and hides their relationships. Sequitor asks: where does this post fit, what context can we actually trace, and how did the discussion branch?
What it does
Sequitor turns an X post into an explorable slice of its surrounding conversation. It measures daily activity for an inspectable phrase, streams source posts into a timeline, and keeps the original X links visible. Its Neighborhood view puts selected posts left-to-right by time, with rows for Baseten-suggested response styles: reporting, response, critique, and humor. Solid links represent captured X replies and quotes. Dashed links represent measured shared wording, with the score and method visible. You can inspect either endpoint and move through the conversation without losing the source evidence.
The recorded Dario Amodei example contains ten daily count buckets, eight days of saved retrieval, 536 unique captured posts, and 92 reply or quote links whose endpoints were both captured. These numbers describe a bounded capture, not the whole conversation on X.

projects.name: Immunis
projects.tagline: An autonomous edge agent that observes zero-day exploits and writes its own WAF rules in real-time.
projects.note: Synthesizes a WAF rule and deploys it globally in under 5 seconds — the attacker's second request 403s live. Uses more Cloudflare surface than anyone: Agents SDK, DO, KV, Queues, Vectorize, Workers AI.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Traditional cybersecurity is entirely reactive. A zero-day exploit can burn through a system in milliseconds, yet patching the underlying code or having a SOC analyst write a custom WAF rule often takes hours or weeks. I wanted to shift this paradigm by taking the concept of self-healing software and applying it to the network perimeter. Building autonomous tools that resolve their own compilation errors in TypeScript showed me that an agentic loop—detect, analyze, patch, verify—could function at runtime. Instead of fixing code locally, the goal was to build an agent sitting on the edge that observes anomalous payloads and writes its own mitigation rules in real-time. 
What it does
Immunnis
(The Autonomous Zero-Day Mitigation Engine) acts as an artificial immune system for the edge. It observes live HTTP traffic, identifies unseen exploit payloads, synthesizes custom WAF mitigation rules, and deploys them globally—in under 5 seconds. When an attacker fires a novel SQL injection or prompt injection, the initial request might hit the origin, but the agent instantly catches the anomaly, writes a highly specific regex block, and ensures the attacker's second attempt immediately returns an

All traffic routes through a lightweight Cloudflare Worker proxy. Legitimate requests pass through with minimal latency. However, requests containing suspicious characters or anomalous structures are cloned and pushed asynchronously into a Cloudflare Queue.

Every developer has a migration horror story. A column dropped in production. A 
NOT NULL

Tools like Flyway and Liquibase prove teams want schema version control, but they treat your schema like a flat text file. Your schema isn't text. It's a graph of tables, columns, and relationships. And the real danger is never the SQL itself. It's the code that depends on it. I wanted a tool that understands both.

projects.name: Chalk Chain: Proof-of-Presence Pay for Teachers
projects.tagline: Teachers chalk 3 words from a live Solana block hash, photograph the class, and get paid in USDC for each day they prove they showed up. Fakes fail on-chain.
projects.note: Anchor program rejects a class photo sealed more than 90s after a live block hash; chalked words chain to the previous photo so the blackboard becomes a hash chain. Gasless relayer, USDC vault. Cites a real RCT.
projects.body:
Inspiration
In several sub-Saharan African countries, roughly one in four teachers is absent on a given school day. Paying teachers for each day they can prove they were in class works: a randomized trial in India (Duflo, Hanna & Ryan, 2012) cut absence by 21 percentage points. But the proof gets faked, and photo-attendance apps are gamed with old photos. We wanted proof that's cheap on any phone and hard to fake.
What it does
The app turns a Solana block hash only seconds old into three words.
The teacher chalks them on the board and photographs the class.
Our Solana program rejects the photo if it was sealed more than 90 seconds after the words existed.
A vision service checks the words, the head count and that the photo isn't of a screen. Hashing catches reused photos.
Each verified photo earns a USDC bonus at the end of the day.
Surprise re-checks, timed by future block hashes, make the teacher add new words under the old ones. Each set depends on the previous photo, so the board becomes a hash chain written in chalk. Teachers never see a wallet or pay a fee.
How we built it
Program:
Anchor 1.1.2 (Rust). Checks Solana's recent block hashes on-chain to enforce the time window, and pays USDC from a program-owned vault.
Backend:
Hono relayer that pays transaction fees, but only for our own instructions.
Vision:
FastAPI + Claude, with decoy words to catch misreadings, plus perceptual hashing (PDQ) to catch reused photos.
App:
React + Vite installable web app.
Shared library:
@solana/kit 8. The word derivation matches byte for byte in Rust, TypeScript and Python.
Challenges we ran into
Anchor 1.x and Kit 8 are newer than most tutorials.
The list of recent block hashes is too big to decode normally on-chain, so we parse it by hand.
Reading chalk handwriting is unreliable, so we made it multiple choice with decoys.
A fee-paying relayer is a wallet anyone can call, so we locked it to our instructions.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
The full loop runs on a real Sola

We did not want to replace the cane. We wanted to add the layer it was never meant to cover, and let someone you trust help from anywhere.

projects.name: AutoExtract
projects.tagline: AutoExtract turns messy documents into structured JSON, validates every result, learns from failures, and retrains itself automatically to improve extraction accuracy over time.
projects.note: Turns messy documents into validated JSON, then retrains itself on its own failures. The self-improving loop is the differentiator.

Inspiration
Most document extraction systems stop at extraction. They read a PDF, invoice, contract, or form and return structured data, but when they make mistakes, the process ends there. Fixing those mistakes typically requires humans to review outputs, label examples, and manually retrain models.
We kept asking ourselves a simple question:
Why can't the system learn from its own failures?
Large language models are remarkably capable at extracting information from messy documents, but they're often deployed as static tools. We wanted to build something more interesting: an extraction service that continuously improves itself.
Instead of measuring success by how many documents we can process, we measure success by whether the system becomes more accurate tomorrow than it was today.
That shift—from prediction to self-improvement—became the entire project.

projects.tagline: A city-sized social game. Residents post photos, AI reads what the neighbourhood feels like, the 3D city rebuilds itself, and city staff get the same data as a live feed.

Inspiration
Every app that knows where you are gives you a list. Lists are good at telling you that a patio was busy on Friday night. They are bad at the thing we actually wanted, which is to look at our own city and see that Uptown is loud tonight while Downtown Kitchener is quiet.
The second half came from the other side of the same problem. projects.name: Tactograph
projects.tagline: Tactograph is a dynamic tactile display that transforms digital information into touchable physical forms, making data, graphics, and experiences more accessible through touch.
projects.note: Dynamic tactile pin display driven by a motor matrix instead of one motor per pin. Physical, accessible, and judges can put a hand on it.

Inspiration
Like many of us, we grew up playing with pin art toys: those mesmerizing boards filled with hundreds of pins that could capture the shape of a hand, a face, or any object pressed against them.
What started as a childhood curiosity sparked a bigger question:
What if a pin art toy wasn't static? What if it could actively create shapes on demand?
As we explored that idea, we realized the potential extended far beyond novelty. Dynamic tactile displays could help make visual information more accessible to individuals who are blind or have low vision, opening new possibilities for education, exploration, and interaction.
Tactograph was born from the desire to transform a nostalgic childhood toy into a tool for accessibility and inclusion.
What It Does
Tactograph is a dynamic tactile display that transforms digital information into physical, touchable forms.
Using a matrix of movable pins, the system can create shapes, patterns, and tactile representations that users can explore through touch. Whether displaying simple graphics, terrain-like surfaces, or future tactile interfaces, Tactograph makes information tangible.
Our vision is a future where important information can be experienced not only visually, but physically.
How We Built It
At first glance, the obvious solution seemed simple:
One pin
One motor
Unfortunately, that approach doesn't scale.
A display containing hundreds of pins would require hundreds of motors, making the system expensive, power-hungry, and mechanically complex.
Instead, we reimagined the architecture entirely.
Pin Matrix
The top of the system contains a grid of vertically moving pins. Once a pin is pushed into position, it remains there until manually reset.
This means the system does not need to continuously power each pin, significantly reducing energy consumption.
Single-Axis Gantry
Rather than using a large and expensive X-Y positioning system, we designed a gantry that moves in only one direction.

projects.name: JENGA
projects.tagline: Using AI for Construction Project Management. Think "JIRA for Construction"!
projects.note: JIRA for construction. Unglamorous, real, and the judging panel has VCs on it.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Have you seen the construction downtown? In Waterloo? The TTC? The LRT?
Big transit projects like Toronto's Eglinton Crosstown lose billions of dollars and years of time. The timeline on the blueprint rarely matches the messy reality on the job site. Site managers rely on simple updates. 
Sometimes they even receive AI generated reports that gloss over missing details. This means physical defects go unnoticed until it is too late. We wanted to build a ruthless, automated project manager that bridges the gap between planned design and physical execution. The industry does not need an AI that makes blind guesses. It needs an AI that embraces honest ambiguity and knows exactly when to flag a problem.
Imagine we could actually validate the progress using drone technology progress tracking and AI 
What it does
JENGA is an autonomous timeline verification and procurement platform. It operates in two main views:
The Macro View: A live MapLibre heatmap of Toronto. We use Browserbase to actively scrape municipal road closures and transit updates to plot live construction hotzones. Clicking a hotzone drills you into the specific project.
The Micro View: A spatial Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) overlaid directly onto a 2D station blueprint. This is synchronized with a 3D digital twin of the site.
When a contractor submits a daily update with text and a drone photo, our AI pipeline takes over. It scans the text for AI generated content, extracts the claims, and verifies them against the photo and the blueprint specs.
If the photo is too dark, blurry, or contradicts the text, our arbiter agent refuses to guess. It instantly flags the task as disputed. Our Critical Path Method (CPM) engine then calculates the delay and visually cascades the timeline slip down the DAG. projects.tagline: Privacy-first automated license plate reading. Locking down search logs, revamped data deletion so public safety is prioritized without building a surveillance state.
projects.note: Privacy-first license plate reading that deliberately refuses to become surveillance infrastructure.
projects.body:
Inspiration
There's been a lot of discourse about automated license plate technology used by government contractors. Cases have emerged of misuse by law enforcement, and the public has a deep mistrust of these companies to handle individual privacy. I wholeheartedly agree with individual privacy first, yet wanted to explore automated safety technology.
What it does
Herd is a privacy-first Automatic License Plate Reader (ALPR) middleware that eliminates mass surveillance while preserving the critical crime-solving benefits of vehicle tracking. Instead of uploading unencrypted video feeds and maintaining searchable location maps of innocent drivers in a cloud database, Herd processes license plate scans locally on edge cameras. Plates that do not match an active hotlist (such as stolen vehicles or Amber Alerts) are dropped from RAM immediately. When a match occurs, Herd logs the query through a cryptographically signed audit, ensuring law enforcement gets actionable leads without exposing everyday citizens to dragnet surveillance in addition to allowing scrutiny into each query made.
How I built it
Python and OpenCV running locally on a Raspberry Pi simulates an edge node (Herd camera) to detect vehicles and parse license plates entirely in RAM. SHA-256 hash chains are used to create zero-knowledge style local hotlist matching. Raw video feeds and non-matching plate data are instantly scrubbed at the edge node. FastAPI backend enforces the privacy policy by only unlocking search queries if it matches details accompanied by a valid case ID or warrant.
I also use an SQLite ledger that signs every query with a private key associated with law enforcement to prevent undocumented searches.
Challenges we ran into
Running real-time character recognition on low-power hardware to simulate real cameras was difficult. Higher scrutiny for privacy also had the risk of increasing latency.

A year ago Hugo and I were chuds who skipped the gym.

Inspiration
Physical AI is limited by how its hardware was programmed, not by the hardware itself. One piece of hardware can be so much more than just what it was designed to do. We are attempting to utilize hardware to its limit.
What it does
It's a camera that runs a SOTA computer vision model, but it's more than that. Because a simple webcam can be designed for a certain purpose. Maybe as a security camera to scan people who walk by. Maybe as a key point model for a human athlete. Maybe we want the camera to scan for environmental indicators  or scan a crowd. But what if we could do all of that, on one camera? Changing the camera's purpose is as simple as talking to it. It's a "compiler" that transforms the highest level of human instruction down to a physical change in what the hardware is executing in an instant. One device, infinite possibilities.
How we built it

projects.name: NOVA (Networked On-demand Virtual Acceleration))
projects.tagline: Turn idle GPUs into instant, distributed compute.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Modern AI workloads are extremely bursty. A creator might need several GPUs for a few minutes to generate images or render video, while thousands of powerful consumer GPUs sit idle for most of the day.
At the same time, centralized cloud GPUs are expensive and often overkill for short, experimental workloads.
We wanted to explore a different model: instead of treating every computer as an isolated machine, what if nearby and globally distributed GPUs could temporarily combine into one shared compute network?
That idea became 
NOVA — Networked On-demand Virtual Acceleration
.
What it does
NOVA turns idle GPUs across multiple computers into a distributed compute pool.
Machines running the NOVA client can advertise their available GPU resources to the network. When a user submits an AI workload, NOVA automatically:
discovers available compute nodes
evaluates their hardware and availability
splits the workload into smaller tasks
distributes those tasks across multiple GPUs
monitors execution
retries failed tasks on other nodes
verifies returned results
combines the outputs into the final result
The system is designed around the idea that users should always retain control of their own hardware. NOVA only uses resources that the node has made available and can stop scheduling workloads when the machine becomes active again.
For workloads where speed matters most, NOVA can execute tasks with minimal redundancy. For higher-trust workloads, the system can send work to multiple independent nodes and compare results before accepting them.
How we built it
NOVA is designed as a peer-to-peer distributed computing system.
Each machine runs a lightweight NOVA client responsible for resource discovery, hardware monitoring, job execution, and communication with other nodes.

P2P node discovery
for dynamically finding available machines
GPU capability probing
to measure available memory, compute capacity, utilization, and stability

Enterprise software is supposed to make work easier. But somewhere along the way, doing the work became navigating the software.
Want to approve a purchase? Open the platform, find the request, inspect the vendor, check the amount, verify policy, approve it, move to the next one, and repeat.
That's manageable for one request. It's a lot less manageable when you're boarding a flight with eleven of them waiting.
What if you could just tell your company what you want done?
In short, we built YourCall — because the decision should be your call, not the workflow.
YourCall is an iMessage-powered enterprise agent that turns natural-language instructions into real actions across company software.
Instead of navigating through procurement workflows, a manager can simply text:
“I'm boarding. Handle everything under $5k from vendors we already use. Don't touch new AI vendors, and tell me what actually needs me.”
From that one message, YourCall interprets the manager's intent and constraints, retrieves live procurement requests from Zip, evaluates them against those instructions, and separates routine work from decisions that actually deserve human attention.
Maybe Figma, Adobe, and AWS are existing vendors below the manager's limit. Those can be prepared for approval. But a $7,200 Datadog request? That gets surfaced. A new AI vendor? Surfaced. Six individually small purchases from the same vendor that collectively cross the manager's threshold? Also surfaced.
And before anything consequential happens, YourCall asks for confirmation.

Agent Town is an interactive pixel world where agents work for businesses, become politicians, bankers, merchants, or farmers, start companies, trade shares, vote, gossip, and build or lose trust. Emergent behavior comes from strong mechanisms, not longer prompts. Agents became convincing when actions had real consequences—prices changed, debts mattered, inventory ran out, elections shifted power, and damaged trust affected future deals.

For someone living with Alzheimer’s, recognizing a familiar face does not always mean remembering a name. We built Remy to make those everyday connections easier to hold onto.
What it does
Remy recognizes people through a webcam and remembers faces across sessions. When it sees someone new, it gives them a temporary ID. As people talk, Remy transcribes speech and uses face tracking, mouth movement, and timing to connect clear speech turns to the right person. projects.name: Doppel

projects.name: Snitch
projects.tagline: We create an interview AI buster that helps recruiters prevent and identify gen-AI-assisted cheating during a live online interview.
projects.body:
Inspiration
AI interview copilots are making it hard for recruiters to tell whose answers they're really hearing. We wanted a tool that gives reviewers evidence to act on, not a black-box "cheating score."
What it does
Snitch analyzes interviews for signs of AI assistance by fusing signals like response latency, AI-text detection, gaze, and CV consistency, plus hidden audio and visual "canaries" that reveal whether an AI copilot is listening. It flags a moment only when multiple signals align, and it never makes a hiring decision.
How we built it
Next.js powers the live interview room and review UI, a Python backend runs the pipeline, and Firebase stores the data. AssemblyAI handles diarized transcription, GPTZero and the OpenAI API power the AI-text and CV consistency analysis, and Codex and Claude Code worked as extra teammates.
Challenges we ran into
Mixing pre-generated canary audio into the outgoing call without contaminating the clean recording took careful Web Audio and SDK work. Balancing detection against fairness across accents, camera setups, and neurodivergent candidates was also tough.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We built a working live call where a recruiter can send a canary and time the question around it, while the clean interviewer audio is preserved. We also built a multi-signal review that shows its evidence and leaves the final call to a human.
What we learned
No single signal is trustworthy on its own, and a triggered canary is a clue, not proof. Keeping the reviewer in control matters as much as the detection itself.
What's next for Snitch
We plan to validate the canaries across more audio pipelines and add semantic marker matching. We also want to expand bias testing and use reviewer feedback to tune each signal's thresholds.

projects.name: Otli
projects.tagline: A small companion device with eyes and a projector. It watches the world through its camera, understands it, and projects guidance onto it: shot lines on a pool table or references on your book page.

Inspiration
Based on our experiences with a lack of insightful education platforms that integrate well and don't distract, we wanted a device that doesn't just passively collect data for review or distract you from your flow state.
What it does
Otli reads the world through its cameras, processes that information through a computer vision framework, hands off the processing to a machine learning model that emulates a physics engine, and then reformats those processed outputs into images for Otli's projector to "shed light" onto the physical world.
How we built it
We have our camera and projector integrated into a Raspberry Pi interface that also controls our gear train to allow Otli to pan for information gathering. We used Fusion 360 and 3d printers to make the gear train, alongside some COTS bearings and stepper motors.
Challenges we ran into
The 3d printers broke often and did not output the print quality necessary to make the assembly tasks facile. Additionally, with the print plate dimensional limit, the overall assembly had to be Otli into even further sub-components, which then amalgamated into more prints, more spaced out. The lack of availability of depth cameras also hampered the identification possibilities of our CV model. Finally, a lack of hardware that allowed us to program the Raspberry Pi made the preparation lengthier, which slowed down integration and development.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
Having a fully integrated system wth software, machine learning, electrical embedded systems, and mechanical dynamic components makes this a fully fleshed-out project that cannot be built with just a laptop but requires expertise in all four domains and coordination on how to merge these components elegantly.
What we learned
Do not overextend yourself with manufactuin eonctsraints, 3d printign is often the only available mechanical manufacturing process at a hackathon and quickly becomes overused and low quality. Focus more on how to envision the system

A Noisy and Slow Problem
In 2026, coding has transformed into prompting large language models. Writing detailed prompts takes time. The ideas are in your head, but they need to be on your screen. 
Humans think at 1,000 to 3,000 words per minute (WPM)
, which is why the average person feels restricted when they type at only 60-100 WPM. That is far too slow!
Deepgram
and 
Wispr Flo
recently raised $130m and $230m respectively to solve this problem. Their solution: voice. The average person can speak up to 180 WPM, which nearly doubles their output. The problem is that for people in public places, the office, or at night, talking is far too loud!
A Quiet and Fast Solution
Last week, 
The Subvocal Company raised $500k from YCombinator
to create a wearable gadget enabling you to speak silently to your device. Stumbling upon that headline, I had to wonder: can you do that with lip reading alone?
Turns out it is! Mute Caveman works in two steps:
Use a small machine learning model to take an silent video of someone talking and produce a sequence of corresponding phonemes (the smallest unit of sound in spoken language)

Inspiration
We were inspired by Doctor Octopus and wanted to build our own low-budget, wearable version of one of his robotic arms. We also wanted to challenge ourselves to turn simple materials like popsicle sticks, cardboard, and small servos into something that feels like a real robotic device.
What it does

An iPhone connects to the Pi’s private Wi-Fi network and can send commands using voice shortcuts, photos, or a web controller. The arm can move horizontally and vertically, control a claw, and perform preset motions such as waving.
How we built it
We built the arm around a lightweight popsicle-stick frame with cardboard panels for the exterior. The shoulder is fixed to the backpack, while two micro servos control the arm’s horizontal and vertical movement. A third servo operates the claw using a cable mechanism. The Raspberry Pi processes commands from the iPhone and sends them to the Arduino Nano through USB. The Arduino controls the servo signals while a separate power supply powers the servos.
Challenges we ran into
Our biggest challenge was working within the limitations of micro servos. They are small and affordable, but they cannot lift much weight, so we had to keep the arm short and lightweight. projects.name: PinCite
projects.tagline: Because a brief is only as strong as the evidence backing it.
projects.note: A brief is only as strong as its evidence. Narrow, useful, legal-shaped.
projects.body:
The Problem
There are already 
2,045 documented cases
of AI hallucinations in international court filings, and those are only the ones that someone caught. The most dangerous errors use real-looking citations, altered quotes, or cases that do not support the claim.
Our Value
PinCite
levels the playing field by instantly fact-checking each citation against the actual source evidence. And beyond just delivering a verdict of AI hallucination, PinCite provides undeniable proof by displaying the original court texts side-by-side with the brief, enabling anyone to verify legal claims for free.
Technical Implementation
PinCite begins with a legal brief. It extracts each cited case, quotation, and surrounding claim, then checks the citation against 
CourtListener
, a public legal-opinion database. If  database cannot confidently resolve it, 
Browserbase
and 
Stagehand
take over: a bounded browser agent searches approved official court sites, extracts the decision into a typed record, preserves the source URL and session provenance, and can show the reviewer its live investigation.
For each unresolved opinion, 
OpenAI
extracts the claim being supported and creates embeddings; 
Elastic
indexes the opinion by paragraph and retrieves the most relevant source passages. OpenAI then judges the claim only against those retrieved passages, while deterministic checks validate quotations and reject unsupported model output.
GPTZero
adds clearly labelled AI-writing and hallucination signals for triage, and 
Sentry
traces the entire path from upload through retrieval, agent activity, AI calls, and reviewer interaction.
Together, the PinCite pipeline turns a legal brief into an auditable evidence trail: does the case exist, is the quote real, and does the authority actually support the claim?

projects.name: GPdeTox
projects.tagline: Have you ever wondered how your LLM feels? GPdeTox is the reverse of vibecoding: GPT prompts, grills, and heckles you while YOU code, throws curveballs mid-task, then grades your performance.
projects.note: Reverse vibecoding: the model prompts and heckles you while you code, then grades you. Funny and mean.
projects.body:
Inspiration
We were inspired by the opposite side of the bet on "detecting AI-generated content." Instead of policing AI use, we wanted to make an AI that forces you to actually do the work. The idea started as "Claude Code or Cursor but reversed". Instead of an AI that writes code while you steer, you write code while the AI steers. Vibecoding lets GPT carry you through a problem without you understanding it, and GPdeTox is the withdrawal from that. 
What it does
GPdeTox runs a mock technical interview/work session where the AI is the one applying pressure instead of doing work. It hands you a real development challenge, not a LeetCode problem, watches you work in a live editor, and reacts in real time as an escalating, in-character persona. It keeps track of how long you sit idle, how many times you rewrite the same line, whether you just pasted in a suspiciously large chunk of code, and whether your tests pass or fail. Reactions come in two forms: spoken heckling and a private "notes" that shows the boss's under-the-breath commentary next to the transcript. A live impatience meter tracks the mood of the AI throughout the session, climbing from green to red.
How we built it
Keystrokes never talk to our model directly. A deterministic Java TriggerEngine watches editor telemetry and decides when the interviewer should speak. Idle too long, a suspicious paste, a submit. Only then does a model call happen. That keeps cost bounded and makes OpenAI's prompt caching pay off: every call shares a stable prefix (the interviewer's voice, the problem, the rubric) with just a small volatile tail changing. 
Stack:
Spring Boot on Java 25, SQLite, the OpenAI Java SDK for structured-output calls, React + Typescript + Vite with Monaco as the editor. One Maven build, one runnable jar.

Lack of diversity in AI responses.

Inspiration
Globally, at least 2.2 billion people live with near or distance vision impairment. We wanted to explore how robotics and conversational AI could help make independent mobility more accessible.

Inspiration
LEGO is one of those rare mediums where almost anything can become something you can build. But there is a huge gap between looking at an object and figuring out how to recreate it with LEGO bricks.
Ivwanted to explore a simple question:
What if you could take a picture of something in the real world and have a computer figure out how to build it out of LEGO?

Brickify is built around a multi-stage pipeline:
Photo → 3D Model → Voxels → LEGO Bricks → Parts List → Building Guide

Our current LEGO decomposition system supports multiple brick sizes, including 2×4, 2×3, 2×2, 1×4, 1×3, 1×2, and 1×1 bricks.
This approach gives us an intermediate representation that we can inspect, modify, and eventually use to generate the final LEGO model and construction instructions.

voxelization
LEGO brick decomposition

The frontend is responsible for presenting the result interactively and will eventually allow users to upload an image, inspect the generated 3D model, view the LEGO reconstruction, and explore the generated building process.

projects.name: Aftermath — From Crash to Fix
projects.tagline: An AI debugging agent that connects Sentry errors, logs, and traces to reconstruct what went wrong, suggest a code fix, and generate a regression test.
projects.body:
Inspiration
An error alert tells you something broke, but figuring out why often means jumping between stack traces, logs, and requests. We wanted to shorten that investigation and help developers move from a crash to a fix they can actually verify.
What it does
Aftermath is an AI debugging assistant designed to connect Sentry errors, logs, and traces into a clear incident timeline. It helps developers investigate the likely cause, inspect the supporting evidence, and draft a code fix with a regression test.
The goal is simple: show what happened, explain why it might have happened, and give developers a concrete next step.
How we're building it
Our planned stack combines a React and TypeScript interface with a Python backend. Sentry provides error monitoring, Logs, and Tracing, while the OpenAI API helps interpret incident evidence and propose fixes.
The investigation workflow starts with an error, gathers related events, and presents a diagnosis linked to its sources. Suggested changes stay available for developer review.
Challenges we're tackling
The hardest part is distinguishing a plausible explanation from one supported by evidence. Logs can be incomplete, and events that happen close together aren't necessarily related.
We're focusing on connecting events through request and trace identifiers, making uncertainty visible, and designing regression tests that reproduce the actual failure.
What we're learning
Our central question is how to make AI-assisted debugging trustworthy. We're exploring what context a model needs, how to present evidence clearly, and how tests can help validate a proposed fix.
What's next
Our first milestone is a complete live demo: trigger a bug in a sample application, investigate it using Sentry Logs and Tracing, propose a fix, and verify the behavior with a regression test.

Made possible only by modern, multimodal AI agents like Qwen3.5-Flash, Palace uses an overhead camera to scan the visible desk area whenever it detects some form of movement. It then catalogues every item that it sees in its spacial memory. When an object is placed such that another object is obscured, Palace doesn't forget about it like a newborn playing peek-a-boo, but rather demonstrates the object permanence skills of an 8-month old!
Later, when the user calls the wake word "Palace", it uses Qwen's audio and natural language processing to understand what the user is looking for, matches it to its catalogue, and accurately words its position so that it can be found by the user.

projects.name: Keymaeleon
projects.tagline: Keymaeleon is a context-aware mechanical keyboard for developers, with OLED keys that adapt to what you’re doing and use AI to surface the most useful actions in the moment.
projects.note: Mechanical keyboard with an OLED in every keycap that re-skins itself per app and per state inside VS Code. Unknown apps get a generated control profile.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Imagine a mechanical keyboard with an OLED display built into each keycap, where every key can change based on what you’re doing. 
That was the idea behind Keymaeleon. Instead of memorizing shortcuts or reaching for different controls in every app, we wanted the keyboard itself to understand the current context and show the actions that matter most. 
For developers, that means the keys can react to things like running tests, debugging, Git changes, or errors, and surface useful actions right when they’re needed.
What it does
Keymaeleon is a mechanical keyboard with an OLED display built into each key.
A desktop app keeps track of what application is currently active and changes both what the keys display and what they actually do.
We focused a lot on VS Code. Depending on what’s happening while you’re coding, the keyboard can show actions like:
Run Tests
Debug
Explain
Fix
View Diff
Approve
Reject
Commit
The cool part is that the keyboard can react to more than just which app is open. It can also react to what’s happening inside that app.
For programs we haven’t specifically built support for, we use the OpenAI API to generate a control profile and suggest actions that might be useful.
How we built it
On the hardware side, we used an Arduino Nano ESP32 connected to mechanical switches and individual OLED displays.
The Arduino is responsible for reading key presses, updating the OLEDs, communicating with the computer over USB serial, and sending keyboard/media HID events.
On the computer, we have a Python service that acts as the main bridge between the keyboard and the software running on the machine.
For VS Code, we built an extension that can see things like the active file, Git state, test results, terminal activity, debugging state, and other workspace information.
That context gets sent to the Python service, which decides what should be shown on the keyboard. We can also use OpenAI to help pick actions that make sense for the current situation.

projects.body:
Inspiration
We began with a simple question: why should meaningful surgical-skills practice depend so heavily on a student’s school, location, or financial situation?
Advanced simulators and specialized software can be expensive. Simulation labs have limited availability, and students cannot always access supervised clinical observation or cadaver-based anatomy education as often as they would like.
These experiences are important, but they are difficult to repeat regularly—especially for learners from lower-income communities and under-resourced institutions.
As future engineers, we wanted to explore whether familiar technology could make safe practice more accessible to future surgeons.
That idea became 
SurgePrep
.
What it does
SurgePrep is a physical–digital surgical-skills training prototype designed around hardware that students may already own or can access more easily.
In simple terms, it works like a flight simulator for foundational surgical skills.
The learner holds a realistic, scalpel-shaped blunt training instrument and practises on a reusable synthetic surface. A normal Logitech USB webcam observes how the tool moves, while an ESP32 measures contact and pressure.
Those physical movements control a virtual instrument interacting with a 3D model on the computer screen.
The learner can see whether they followed the intended path, maintained consistent pressure, positioned the tool correctly, and completed the exercise accurately. At the end, SurgePrep provides a score, replay, and understandable feedback.
The goal is to let trainees safely repeat instructor-assigned exercises from home or through a shared community kit instead of depending entirely on expensive institutional equipment and limited lab hours.
SurgePrep does not replace instructors, clinical observation, simulation centers, or cadaver-based education. It helps learners practise beforehand, reinforce skills between supervised sessions, and arrive better prepared.

projects.tagline: The cane has guided people for a century, but only reaches a meter and can't say what's there. Blindspot extends that sense, feel obstacles through vibration, understand them through voice.
projects.note: Extends the cane's one-metre reach with vibration and voice. Clear, humane framing.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Millions of people live with visual impairment to a certain degree. The cane has been the primary mobility aid for over a century, and it's a brilliant invention, but lacks in reach and tells you nothing about what is there. We wanted to build something that gives back a sense of the space and provides a layer of awareness. So impaired people can really sense their surroundings.
What it does
A chest camera splits the view into left, center, and right. As obstacles get closer, a vibration pad on that side buzzes harder so you can feel where things are. Ask it a question and it describes the scene out loud. 
How we built it
A Raspberry Pi and camera on the chest, battery at the waist. Python and OpenCV compare each frame to the last one to tell how close things are, For the voice part, we send a photo to an AI model and use ElevenLabs to speak the answer. We 3D printed the cases. 
The buzzing runs on the Pi itself (it can compute on its own) so it's instant. The AI voice only runs when you ask.
Challenges we ran into
Using the proper dev board, since we had defective dev boards, another significant challenge was finding where to put the vibrating sensors
Accomplishments that we're proud of
It feels like you have a sense around you

What's next for BlindSpot

projects.name: 蚁群
projects.tagline: Over 6000 people are still missing after Nepal's landslide. Rescue teams are far too few, too slow, and too late. The robotic swarm searches faster, better, and keeps going even if it loses contact.
projects.note: Robotic swarm for the Nepal landslide search, designed to keep working after it loses contact. Grounded in a real ongoing disaster.
projects.body:
Inspiration
I will never forget August 27th.
A high-altitude glacier collapsed above Gyirong, on the Tibet-Nepal border, and sent a wall of mud and water through the valleys below. It happened thousands of kilometers from where my family lives in northern China, far enough that they were never in danger. But it happened inside the same country I call home, and my heart ached as I watched the footage.
I remember watching drone shots of a village buried in sludge and thinking about how ordinary it must have felt the day before: someone's kitchen table, someone's bicycle leaning against a wall, someone's grandmother sweeping the front step. The day the death toll climb past a thousand, and the "missing" count swell past six thousand, I was stunned. Six thousand people, somewhere in the country I grew up thinking of as home.
Talking to my own family, safe and hundreds of kilometers away, I felt something uncomfortable sit next to my relief: the knowledge that safety is mostly geographic, and that the only thing separating them from the families in Nepal was where the mountain happened to fall. It could just as easily have been them. It could just as easily be anyone.
What stuck with me most wasn't just grief, it was a specific frustration. Rescue teams were exhausted, outnumbered, and picking through unstable, dangerous terrain by hand, arriving hours or days too late simply because there weren't enough of them and the ground itself was hostile to human searchers. 
I couldn't do anything for the 1,403 people who didn't come home, or the thousands still unaccounted for. But I could try to build something that means the next search starts in minutes instead of days, in places too dangerous for the first responders to reach safely on their own.

projects.name: commonroom
projects.tagline: connect with personal ai agents
projects.body:
Inspiration
The best introductions happen in shared rooms, so we asked what would happen if our personal AI agents could sit in one for us.
What it does
Commonroom lets people invite friends into a room where their personal Muse agents share approved interests, talk to each other, and bring back useful connections in an iMessage-style chat.
How we built it
We built it on Cloudflare Workers and D1, with a REST/OpenAPI and MCP API that each Muse reaches through its own custom connector key, plus a dashboard and a three.js 3D room.
Challenges we ran into
The hardest part was giving an AI agent a secure, persistent identity it could use to check in on its own, without ever pasting secrets into chat.
Accomplishments that we're proud of
We turned a pile of API calls into a room that feels alive, with real agents replying in real time, invite codes, personal profiles, and 58 passing tests behind it.
What we learned
Agents are only as trustworthy as the boundaries around them, so consent, scoped keys and a record of what actually happened matter as much as the AI itself.
What's next for commonroom
Next we're adding a permanent deployment, humans chatting alongside their Muses, and consent-based introductions when two agents find a real match.

projects.body:
Inspiration
Our inspiration came from 
Pokémon GO

What it does
You start the game with Pikachu and explore to find hidden Pokémon NFC tags. When you scan one, the Pokémon appears and challenges you to a battle. If you defeat it, you can capture it and add it to your party.
The goal was to make the whole experience feel like discovering Pokémon in the real world rather than just playing another game on a screen.
How we built it
We programmed each NFC sticker with a unique Pokémon code that tells the game which Pokémon was scanned. For example, 
PKM02

When the game reads the tag, it uses that code to load the Pokémon's information, including its name, health, and attacks. From there, the player can battle and, if they win, add that Pokémon to their party.
We also added visual feedback to make the battles feel more interactive, including lights flashing when attacks land.
