projects.name: HyperDrive-badge
projects.tagline: HyperDrive Badge powers a hacker badge with a $3 rechargeable flashlight and 3D printed AA inserts. Charge while using it, skip battery swaps, and reduce disposable battery waste.
projects.body:
Last year, I was walking home from E7 in the dark and wished I had a flashlight. This year, I brought a $3 Dollarama flashlight and attached it to my hacker badge for the walk home. But the flashlight needed charging, and the badge needed fresh AA batteries every few hours. That got me thinking: could I use the flashlight’s rechargeable battery to power the badge?
HyperDrive Badge replaces the badge’s disposable AA batteries with power from a rechargeable flashlight. Instead of swapping batteries every few hours, I can recharge the flashlight, including while using the badge. It makes the badge more convenient to use and reduces disposable battery waste.
I removed the flashlight’s bulb and wired its power source to the badge. I then 3D printed two AA-shaped inserts with space for wires. These fit into the badge’s existing battery compartment as drop-in replacements, connecting it to the flashlight’s rechargeable power source.
The main challenge was connecting the flashlight’s power source through the badge’s existing AA battery compartment. The printed inserts needed to fit properly and leave enough room for the wires.
I turned a $3 flashlight into a reusable power source for my hacker badge. The 3D printed inserts let me use the existing battery compartment, and I no longer need to keep replacing disposable batteries.
This project taught me how repurposing everyday electronics and designing simple 3D printed parts can solve a practical problem. A useful hardware hack does not have to start with expensive components; it can start with something you already have.
I’d like to refine the printed inserts, make the wiring more secure, and test how long the badge runs on a full charge. I’d also like to explore bringing back the flashlight function, so it can power my badge and light my walk home.

projects.name: AndroidRelay
projects.tagline: Android Relay gives AI agents fast, safe control of Android apps. Instead of slow, chat-by-chat ADB connections and fragile scripts, it provides an interface for agents to interact with devices.
projects.body:
About the project
Android Relay was inspired by a simple frustration: AI agents can reason about software, but interacting with a real Android device is still slow, brittle, and often tied to app-specific automation scripts. We wanted to make Android interaction feel more like a general computer-use capability: an agent should be able to inspect the current UI, reason about it, act safely, and verify the result across many apps.
We built a local Android MCP controller on top of ADB and UI hierarchy capture. It exposes generic operations for observing the device, finding UI elements, clicking, typing, launching apps, waiting for state changes, and verifying results. Instead of hardcoding Discord or any other app, the agent works from accessibility metadata such as text, descriptions, resource IDs, hierarchy context, and editable fields.
Latency became the central challenge. Full UI observations were expensive, and repeated agent-to-tool round trips made simple actions take far too long. We added hierarchy-only observations, compact tool responses, cached launcher resolution, atomic text-entry verification, and server-side multi-step navigation transactions. The controller can now resolve a known route, confirm the destination field, send text, and verify the result in one bounded operation.
We also learned that safety and speed have to be designed together. A fast tap is not enough if the UI has changed or two controls have the same label. Android Relay rejects ambiguous selectors, verifies the exact target field before text entry, and confirms post-action state rather than treating ADB dispatch as success.
Finally, we built a shared local controller daemon. Earlier versions started a new ADB controller for every chat, which caused reconnect overhead and device-ownership conflicts. projects.body:
Inspiration
We wanted to make typing on the web faster and more effortless. Carat predicts the next action a user is likely to take and lets them accept it with one keypress.
What it does
Carat predicts what you'll type next, using the context of the page and your recent activity to offer short, relevant completions. Pressing one key accepts the suggestion, so you can move faster without interrupting your flow.
How we built it
We built Carat as a browser-based autocomplete assistant that uses page context and recent activity to generate concise, context-aware suggestions. We focused on making the interaction light.
Challenges we faced
The biggest challenge was making suggestions useful without being distracting. We had to balance context, recency, and brevity while ensuring that Carat only completes what the user is likely to type next. We learned that the best suggestions are short, relevant, and easy to accept. Next, we would like to improve personalization and support more browsers.

Inspiration
Planning an event should feel exciting, but it often becomes overwhelming. Organizers have to balance venues, vendors, budgets, schedules, guests, and constant last-minute changes. We wanted to create a tool that gives every organizer a reliable planning partner—one that turns chaos into a clear path forward.
What it does
EventPilot is an AI event-planning agent that transforms a simple event brief into an actionable plan. It can create schedules, organize budgets, suggest vendors, identify potential conflicts, and keep important event details in one place. Its goal is to help organizers spend less time coordinating and more time creating memorable experiences.
How we built it
We designed EventPilot around a simple conversational workflow. Users describe their event, goals, budget, timeline, and requirements in plain language. The agent then structures that information into key planning areas, including tasks, timelines, costs, and recommendations. We focused on making the experience straightforward, so users can get useful guidance without needing to learn a complicated planning system.
Challenges we ran into
One of our biggest challenges was deciding how much information the agent should ask for without making planning feel like filling out a long form. We also had to think about how to present recommendations clearly while recognizing that every event has different priorities. Balancing flexibility with useful structure was central to the project.

projects.name: BtOS
projects.tagline: AI coding agents stop where the OS starts. We built an autonomous IP-KVM, a hardware layer that gives an AI agent eyes and hands before an operating system is even running.
projects.note: An autonomous IP-KVM giving an agent eyes and hands before an operating system has booted. Goes where coding agents structurally cannot.
projects.body:
Inspiration
AI coding agents today are remarkably capable, but only inside an OS. They can write code, browser the internet, run terminal commands, even debug a stack trace. But the moment something breaks below the OS (a corrupted bootloader, a BIOS setting that needs changing, an OS reinstall) the agent is helpless, because there's no operating system for it to act inside. That's still a human walking to a data center with a monitor and keyboard.
What it does
IP-KVM (IP-based keyboard/video/mouse) already solves remote access to this problem, it's the standard tool sysadmins use to see and control a server over the network when SSH isn't an option. But it's still a human doing the clicking. We want to build the next step: an autonomous IP-KVM, where a vision-capable AI agent can watch the and any issues behind the OS.

projects.name: SCOUT-E
projects.tagline: an embodied multimodal search rover
projects.body:
Our Story
We were inspired by a simple question: 
what if robots could understand people the way people understand each other?
Instead of controlling a robot through rigid commands, we wanted to build something that could see its surroundings, listen to what someone says, ask questions, and act on natural human intent.
We’re currently building a small mobile robot powered by a Raspberry Pi 5, cameras, and motor controllers. Our goal is to combine real-time vision, speech, and language so the robot can navigate its environment and interact with people naturally. Right now, we’re focused on getting the core perception, conversation, and movement loop at least functional.
Next, we’re bringing those pieces together into a complete experience: the robot will receive a natural-language request, visually search its environment, clarify what it sees when necessary, and physically act on the conversation. Ultimately, we want to explore what happens when interacting with a robot feels less like programming a machine and more like communicating with a teammate.

projects.tagline: Camera-guided posture and movement feedback for everyday life.
projects.body:
Inspiration
“Sit up straight” is easy advice to give and hard to apply. We wanted something more useful: a way to look at how we sit, carry a bag, or move, then understand what we could try changing.
Align started with the idea of making posture and mobility guidance easier to use in everyday life.
What it does
Align is a mobile app for guided posture and movement checks. Users take photos from suggested angles or record a short movement, then receive plain-language feedback on what is visible.
Someone carrying a shoulder bag could compare their stance with and without it. Someone working at a desk could look at their setup and try an adjustment.
Our planned features include:
Camera outlines to help users capture useful views.
Visual explanations tied to observations in their photos.
Simple posture, mobility, and ergonomic suggestions.
Before-and-after comparisons so users can see what changed and record how it feels.
We aim to base the guidance on reputable healthcare and ergonomic resources. Align is an educational wellness tool, not a medical assessment or diagnosis.
How we're building it
We're planning an Expo and React Native app with guided camera capture and AI-assisted image analysis. The app will connect visible observations with a small collection of reference guidance and explain possible adjustments.
We also plan to add spoken instructions and follow-up questions so users can interact with the app while positioning themselves away from the phone.
Challenges we're working through
Camera angle and clothing can change how posture appears in a photo. The app needs to recognize when a view is insufficient and ask for another capture.
We're also working on keeping the feedback specific without treating one body position as the ideal for everyone.
What we're proud of
Our focus is a simple interaction: capture a view, understand an observation, and try one adjustment. We want users to see what the feedback refers to instead of having to interpret a long report.

projects.name: Hands-on learning
projects.tagline: Learn how everyday machines work through interactive 3D experiments. Change parts, test predictions, and get AI guidance grounded in what actually happens.
projects.body:
Inspiration
Reading an explanation of a machine can leave you wondering whether you really understand it. We wanted to make that understanding tangible: change something, predict what will happen, and watch the result.
Hands-On Learning explores how interactive 3D experiments and an AI tutor can help people understand everyday mechanisms.
What we're building
Our first learning experience focuses on bicycle gears.
Learners will explore a simplified 3D drive train, adjust gear combinations, and compare how those changes affect wheel rotation. Before running an experiment, they will predict the outcome. The tutor will then explain the result using their chosen configuration.
The core learning loop is: explore, predict, experiment, and explain.
## Planned implementation
We plan to use Three.js and React Three Fiber for the interactive visualization, with application code calculating the mechanical relationships.
An AI tutor will guide experiments through predefined, validated actions. Backboard is our planned integration for conversations, lesson context, and learning history.
The tutor will receive simulation results so its feedback refers to what happened in the experiment. AI output will not execute arbitrary JavaScript or generate the simulation's rules.
## Key challenges
The main challenges are keeping the mechanical behavior accurate, making the 3D controls intuitive, and connecting explanations to the learner's actions.
We are starting with one mechanism so we can focus on a complete learning experience.
## Current status
The project is in development. This initial submission describes the intended MVP; implementation details and results will be updated before final judging.
## What's next
After completing the first lesson, we hope to add reassembly challenges, fault diagnosis, and a shareable experiment notebook.

Inspiration
What it solves
CI proves your code compiles and that the tests someone already wrote still pass. It proves nothing about the thing you just built.
Three gaps follow from that:
New code is the least tested code.
A feature shipped an hour ago has no test coverage by definition. The tests that exist were written for the behaviour that existed before. Coverage is inversely correlated with risk.
Nobody writes end-to-end tests under deadline.
They are slow to write, slow to run, and brittle. On a small team they are the first thing cut and the last thing restored.
Preview deploys are a link, not a verdict.
Vercel tells you the build succeeded and hands you a URL. Whether the signup flow still works is left as an exercise for whoever clicks it, which on a fast-moving team is often nobody until a user complains.

projects.name: Skim

projects.body:
About the project
As more AI agents use reusable skills, we noticed a problem: installing a new skill can introduce instructions that conflict with skills already in use. It can be hard to see which instructions an agent will follow, or to restore the previous setup if the new skill does not work out. That inspired us to build a skill manager with conflict detection and an Undo button.
Our planned system imports complete 
SKILL.md
folders into a shared registry. Before installation, it compares the new skill with active skills, highlights conflicting instructions and their source lines, and lets the user choose which skill should apply. It records the resulting configuration as a Git commit. Multiple agents can then load the same version; if the user undoes the installation, the system creates a new commit that restores the earlier configuration.
We learned that a skill can include scripts and reference files beyond 
SKILL.md
, and that detecting a meaningful conflict requires checking whether two instructions apply to the same task. Our main challenges are making those conflict reports precise and verifying that Undo restores agent behavior, not just files. We are testing both with a pair of skills that prescribe different package managers for the same task.
Built with
Agent Skills (
SKILL.md
), Git, OpenAI API, and a shared skill registry. Additional framework and hosting technologies will be listed once implemented.

tracks.name: OpenAI API Prizes
tracks.crit: What the OpenAI API powers, plus one concrete way Codex improved your build.

tracks.name: Cloudflare: Best Agent with a Brain
tracks.crit: Workers as the agent's backend brain, with memory, tools, state, workflows or real-world actions.

tracks.name: Solana: Best Use of Solana
tracks.crit: A creative, genuinely on-chain use of the Solana ecosystem.

tracks.name: Solana: Best Badge Hack
tracks.crit: Anything built on or with the Hack the North badge itself.

tracks.name: Linq: Best Use of Linq
tracks.crit: New utilities and experiences brought directly into iMessage.

tracks.name: Rox: Best AI Agent
tracks.crit: Agents on real-world messy data: conflicting sources, incomplete records, decisions under uncertainty.

tracks.name: Baseten: Best Use of Baseten
tracks.crit: A creative way to put Baseten inference or training into the build.

tracks.name: Warp: Best Developer Tool
tracks.crit: Meaningfully improves any part of the development lifecycle. No API requirement.

tracks.name: Elastic: Find the Signal
tracks.crit: Agentic systems with Elasticsearch as the context layer over genuinely messy data.

tracks.name: Browserbase: Best Use of Browserbase
tracks.crit: AI automating real work on the web on a human's behalf.

tracks.name: Shopify: Hack Shopping with AI
tracks.crit: Technical innovation where AI meets commerce. Make them say 'wait, that's possible?'

tracks.name: QNX: Embedded System with AI
tracks.crit: A cannot-fail embedded application on QNX with AI running on the hardware, not the cloud.

tracks.name: Bracket Bot: Best Use of Hardware
tracks.crit: A sick demo where the robot is essential to the idea.

tracks.name: Federato: Insurance Agent
tracks.crit: An agent that ingests submissions, enriches them with risk data and reasons against carrier appetite.

tracks.name: Sentry: Best Use of Sentry
tracks.crit: Two or more Sentry products beyond error monitoring, shaping what you actually built.

tracks.name: Dryft: Fastest Token Generation
tracks.crit: Make an autoregressive transformer generate tokens as fast as possible on H100s. Correctness first.

tracks.name: Dominion Dynamics: WHITEOUT
tracks.crit: Shared intelligence coordinating a heterogeneous fleet to find and track a moving target.

tracks.name: Huawei: openJiuwen Multi-Agent
tracks.crit: Genuine multi-agent collaboration: decomposition, communication, tool use, coordination.

tracks.name: Tether: Best Sovereign App
tracks.crit: Local-first AI built on QVAC and Pear.

tracks.name: Zip: Best Use of Zip
tracks.crit: Procurement an enterprise would genuinely want. One strange idea that half works beats a polished obvious one.

tracks.name: Expo: Best Mobile Experience
tracks.crit: A mobile app that is beautiful, feels truly native, and is a joy to use.

tracks.name: MLH: Best Use of ElevenLabs
tracks.crit: Natural, emotionally expressive generated voice at the centre of the experience.

tracks.name: MLH: Best Use of Gemini API
tracks.crit: Push the boundaries of what Gemini can do in a hack.

tracks.name: Aramco: Best Beginner Hack
tracks.crit: Excellence from a team where every member has attended one hackathon or fewer.

tracks.name: Composio: Best Agent with Composio
tracks.crit: The most ambitious agent built on Composio's integrations and delegated auth.

tracks.name: Backboard.io: Built on Backboard
tracks.crit: We judge ambition. The more of the stack you use, the crazier it gets, the better your odds.

tracks.name: GPTZero: Best Use of GPTZero API
tracks.crit: Protect the authenticity of information using AI and hallucination detection.

tracks.name: Cognition: Best Use of Devin
tracks.crit: The most interesting and technically impressive project built with Devin.

tracks.name: Intact: Quoting Interface of the Future
tracks.crit: Reimagine how people get car or tenant insurance, with accessibility front and centre.

tracks.name: RBC: Signal in the Noise
tracks.crit: An agent harness over massive financial research that adapts to a surprise dataset live.

tracks.name: CSE: Log & Order
